prompt.context: Your client is a US storage company that rents out storage space at its own facilities. It is considering entering into the commercial portable storage market where it would deliver the storage unit to the customer, allow them to rent it for as long as they need it, and then pick up the container when they are done with it. Storage containers are old freight shipping containers. Assume entry into 1 test market. Assume that this is a new offering so the client would capture 100% of the market share.
prompt.question: Your objective is to determine if the company should enter this market.

clarifying_info.q: What is the revenue structure for the portable storage offering?
clarifying_info.a: 80% of pods are utilized. Average length of contract is 10 weeks. Price is $300 per week. Each pod is utilized all year (5 cycles per year).

Acquisition cost is $15,000 per unit; 400 units are needed. Transportation cost is $4 per mile with an average of 500 miles per rental round trip. Storage cost is $200,000 per year. Overhead is $100,000 per year.

exhibits.title: Cost Details
exhibits.shows: A table listing cost input assumptions for the portable storage business
exhibits.data: Acquisition cost = $15k per unit; 400 units needed; Transportation = $4 per mile, avg 500 miles; Storage cost = $200k per year; Overhead = $100k per year

exhibits.title: Calculations Table

exhibits.data: Rows: Storage Unit Acquisition, Transportation, Storage Costs, Overhead, Total Costs; Revenue rows: # of Units 320, contract length 10 weeks, price $300/week, 5 cycles/yr; Total Revenue $4,800,000/yr; Total Costs Y1 $9,500,000, annually Y2-Y5 $3,500,000, 5-yr total $23,500,000; 5-yr Revenue $24,000,000

framework: Market sizing: identify target customers and estimate demand for portable storage
Revenue model: price per week, utilization rate, contract length, annual cycles
Cost structure: unit acquisition, transportation, storage, overhead
Profitability analysis: year 1 vs. multi-year payback
Market entry recommendation and expansion strategy

questions.prompt: Who are the target customers for this portable storage offering? Brainstorm customer segments.
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify commercial customers across multiple verticals. Key segments: Retail (seasonal inventory overflow), Manufacturing (temporary storage during expansion or relocation), Office moves (storage during transitions), Small businesses with seasonal demand spikes. Candidate should think broadly across industries with temporary, bulky, or overflow storage needs.

questions.prompt: How might we identify demand for this offering?
questions.guidance: Acceptable approaches include: monitoring competitors in the portable storage market to gauge existing demand; analyzing existing customer contracts to identify short-term contracts, contracts using very little space, or customers storing large items infrequently — these are proxies for portable storage demand.

questions.prompt: What might be some of the costs of this business?
questions.guidance: Candidate should cover both capital and operating cost categories. Key cost buckets: Acquisition of storage units, Storage/yard costs, Labor (loading/unloading), Trucking/transportation, Marketing, Management/overhead, Insurance, Utilities.

questions.prompt: Calculate the revenue and costs for the portable storage business over 5 years. Is this a profitable venture?
questions.guidance: Candidate should systematically work through the cost table and revenue model. Effective units = 400 x 80% = 320. Revenue per unit per year = 5 cycles x 10 weeks x $300 = $15,000. Total annual revenue = 320 x $15,000 = $4,800,000. Y1 costs include one-time acquisition. Y2-Y5 are operating costs only. 5-yr total revenue ($24M) slightly exceeds 5-yr total costs ($23.5M), so the investment pays back over 5 years.

math.setup: Effective units = 400 units x 80% utilization = 320 units. Revenue per unit/yr = 5 cycles x 10 weeks x $300/week = $15,000. Transportation cost per unit/yr = $4/mile x 500 miles x 5 rentals = $10,000.
steps: Storage Unit Acquisition (Y1 only) = 400 units x $15,000 = $6,000,000
math.answer: Y1 is unprofitable (-$4,700,000). The business achieves simple payback over 5 years with a cumulative profit of $500,000.

questions.prompt: What might be some ways of increasing the margin for this business?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates think across revenue and cost levers. Revenue: offer lower prices for longer-term contracts to improve utilization and reduce churn; repeat/loyal customer pricing to drive retention. Cost: decrease overhead through operational efficiency; acquire units more cheaply (e.g., sourcing from overseas manufacturers); optimize routing to reduce average miles per rental.

brainstorming.prompt: What might be some ways of increasing the margin for this portable storage business?

categories.name: Revenue levers
ideas: Lower prices for longer-term contracts to incentivize multi-cycle customers
Repeat customer pricing / loyalty discounts to retain high-volume users
Upsell ancillary services (locks, packing supplies, loading labor)

categories.name: Cost reduction
ideas: Decrease overhead costs through leaner operations
Acquire storage units more cheaply (overseas sourcing, bulk purchase discounts)
Optimize delivery routing to reduce average miles per rental
Negotiate volume discounts with trucking providers

recommendation: Enter the portable storage market in the single test market
Year 1 will be cash-flow negative due to upfront unit acquisition cost ($6M), but the business is profitable on a simple 5-year payback basis (cumulative net profit of $500,000 over 5 years)
Long-term, expand into additional geographic markets once the test market validates the model
risks: Actual utilization may fall below 80%, significantly compressing revenue
Transportation costs are sensitive to fuel prices and actual mileage — if avg miles exceed 500, margins erode quickly
Competitive response if other players enter the market before expansion
Capital intensity of acquisition ($6M upfront) requires strong balance sheet or financing
next_steps: Validate 80% utilization assumption through pilot demand research in the test market
Identify markets where demand is high and average mileage is low to prioritize expansion
Explore cheaper unit acquisition options (overseas sourcing) before full rollout
Consider discounted cash flow analysis to account for time value of money before final capital commitment
